left381000Blast: to build (builder cells, make things).
Clast: to destroy (reabsorb tissue, breaks things)

Blasts and clasts are constantly working together to change the bone tissue. They respond to changes in the amount of calcium in the body (because bones store calcium) and they also respond to changes in the amount of force on the body.
So if your body has to hold up MORE force, the bones must get stronger/denser, and if your body needs to hold up LESS force, the bones CAN get less dense
Cyte: a generic cell, helps to maintain and keep bone alive, but does not create or destroy bone.
Compact bone has circular osteon arranged together, kind of like spaghetti that is stacked together in a bundle. The blood supply is in the centre of the osteon.

left10901800Spongy or trabecular (branching) bone provides support inside the bone, but is porous and light, to allow the bones to be a manageable weight but still have internal support from impact. The spongy bone is kind of like those dried noodle cakes that you have in instant noodles!
Both compact and spongy bone have the rings of bone tissue with osteocytes and canaluci, the compact bone blood supply is in the middle, and the spongy bone is surrounded by blood.
46191-19600100Epiphysis – the ends of a long bone, edges of compact bone and the centre in spongy bone. This is the classic organisation of bone tissue.
Epiphyseal plate – this is made of cartilage in kids and is what allows bones to grow.
Diaphysis – the shaft of a long bone, has a cavity that is filled with bone marrow – red from making blood cells, and yellow in adults that stores fat mostly.
Bones are HIGHLY vascular – lots and lots of blood!!
Joins the broken ends of the bone together
Woven immature bone (bone tissue without the structure of compact bone) replaces the cartilage
Woven, immature bone becomes mature structured compact bone with is designed to withstand the forces of the bone.
Holds the bones in the right place for repair – provides some support
Bone is stronger than cartilage but still weak (the bone is not continuous yet)
Restores the function and structure from before the bone was broken.

Remodelling uses osteoblasts and clasts to remove older bone and replace with new bone. This process happens all the time anyway, in repair, it is breaking down WOVEN IMMATURE BONE and replacing it with NEW COMPACT BONE, thus restoring normal structure and function.

Bone is constantly being remodelling – this is when the osteoclasts reabsorb bone and osteoblasts make new bone. In this image, the black osteons are older and some have been absorbed by osteoclasts, with osteoblasts making the newer bone where the old bone has been removed.
The black osteons would be older osteons. The blue and red ones would be newer, and the green one would be the newest – they are often overlapping to make them stronger!
This remodelling can occur for lots of reasons. Some examples are:
When you get heavier, the bones experience more stress and so build denser bones that are better designed to hold your weight
When you get lighter, the bone doesn’t need to be as dense!
If you have extra calcium, your body can make MORE bones and your osetoblasts increase in activity to store the extra calcium away as bones

If you lack calcium in your blood, your osteoclasts can break down bones to release the calcium from the bone into the blood to get it back up to normal for other parts of your body to use it (your brain, heart and your muscles need calcium to work properly!)
If you are lifting weights for example, that places stress on the body – the muscles get bigger to better lift the weight, and the bones remodel to better support the weights.
The opposite occurs if you stop lifting weights – the body is a “use it or lose it” kind of machine – it only does what it HAS to.
Adults vs kids bones – the bones of children are more immature – the ends are still flexible and cartilaginous to allow for growth!

Motor fibres have their cell bodies in the grey matter of the spinal cord. Sensory fibres have their cell bodies in the ganglion of the dorsal root (in the red). The ventral root (the blue) doesn’t need a ganglion as the cell bodies are in the spinal cord.

Pyramidal tracts – the Upper Motor Neurons that brig information down to the spinal cords from the motor cortex. The somatic nervous system has a 2 neuron set up = Upper and Lower Motor Neurons. You will also see a 2 neuron set up in the Autonomic nervous system – pre and post ganglionic fibres.

Static Paralysis – muscles still have reflexes, but you can’t consciously move your muscles. This is because the lower motor neuron which controls reflexes is still functional, so that means the upper motor neuron must be damaged
Flaccid Paralysis – muscles have no reflexes, and you can’t consciously move your muscles. The lower is definitely damaged and not functional, the upper motor neuron may or may not be functional.
Para/Quadriplegia – Paralysis due to damage to the spinal cord – the spinal cord level determines the functions that are lost.
Hemiplegia – Paralysis due to damage to the motor cortex of the brain, and effects half the body – left or right!

Antagonistic pairs are pairs of muscles that perform the opposite movements, and are the agonist/antagonist pairs for each different movement. Generally you’ll find antagonistic pairs on opposite sides of the body.
For example, biceps and triceps are an antagonistic pair.

During forearm flexion (bending your arm at the elbow), biceps in shortening, and triceps is relaxing/lengthening to allow this movement. In this case, biceps is the agonist (prime moving, causing the movement) and triceps is the antagonist (opposes/does the opposite movement).

During forearm extension (straightening your arm at the elbow), biceps is relaxing/lengthening and triceps is shortening. In this case, biceps is the antagonist (opposes/does the opposite movement) and triceps is the agonist (prime mover, causing the movement).

What determines blood pressure? You’ll need to think about our physiology as well as those factors that can change our blood pressure.
High blood pressure is defined as?
High blood pressure has several chronic, downstream consequences. What are they? Thinking about the implications for long term health and wellness, as well as why we care as nurses!

You have nervous system processes that help to keep your blood pressure steady at rest, and help to increase or decrease it back to normal for exercise or after exercise, based on feedback from your body. We are going to focus on regulation – how your body RETURNS blood pressure to normal after it has been changed.

How does the nervous system detect and return blood pressure to normal when it is lower than normal (e.g. you’ve just stood up quickly and BP to your brain drops; think gravity – as for Jack’s postural hypotension)
How is this process different when it is higher than normal (e.g. after a run, after a fright, etc)
You also have renal system processes that use hormones to help return low blood pressure to normal over the long term.

The human body has what is called set points – this is where the body maintains homeostasis to, what your body thinks is normal. These set points will be slightly different between people. Sometimes, if your body has something that is constantly outside the normal range (e.g. if your BP is always high), your body changes its set point (it kind of goes, ahh fine, this is what normal is now) to your new normal. This is similar to when people from Dunedin laugh when Aucklanders say it’s cold, and they’re like, THIS ISNT COLD UNTIL YOUR TOILET IS FROZEN, GET IN THE BIN YOU WUSS. These two individuals have different ‘set points’ about what is cold.

NCNZ Standards of Competence to cover in Science courses
3.8: Provides, receives and responds appropriately to constructive feedback.
This course will lay the foundations of scientific knowledge required for future nursing practice including the basic structure, concepts and principles that underpin functioning of the human body.
The purpose of this course is to continue the development of the scientific knowledge required for future nursing practice.
The purpose of this course is to examine and apply Maatai Oranga (Health Science) in relation to Tikanga aa-Tapuhi.
On successful completion of this course, students will be able to:
LO1 : Explain the structure and function of a range of human body systems to support safe nursing practice.
LO2 : Analyse the principles of homeostasis in maintaining physiological balance relevant to nursing care.
LO3 : Describe the support, coordination and control of movement in the human body within a nursing context.
LO4 : Apply knowledge of human genetics and inheritance to nursing assessment and care planning.
LO5 : Demonstrate knowledge of the regulatory and integrative functions of the human body including sensory functions, to underpin nursing practice.
On successful completion of this course, students will be able to:
LO1 : Explain the structure and function of a range of body systems
LO2 : Discuss the principles of homeostasis.
LO3 : Describe the support, coordination, and control of movement in the human body
LO4 : Explain the fundamentals of human genetics and inheritance
LO5 : Demonstrate knowledge of the regulatory and integrative functions of the human body, including sensory functions.

1. Describe the function of cardiovascular system.
2. Describe the structural and functional differences between the artery, vein and capillary.
3. Outline the factors involved in capillary fluid movement – including hydrostatic and oncotic pressures.
4. Describe the relationship between blood pressure, blood flow, and peripheral resistance, and velocity of blood flow .
5. Describe the functional anatomy of the heart and the major blood vessels of the heart. Be able to describe:
5.1 Location and orientation of the heart
5.3 The structure and function of the heart walls, chambers and valves
6. Describe the blood flow through the heart, systemic circuit, pulmonary circuit, and coronary circulation.
7. Describe the sounds the heart makes and the best places where the sounds can be detected.
8. Describe the generation and conduction of the basic rhythm of heart in relation to cardiac cycle and electrocardiogram.
9. Discuss the homeostatic mechanisms involved in the control of heart rate, stroke volume and cardiac output (both neural and hormonal control).
10. Explain the effect of general factors on heart rate, stroke volume and cardiac output.
11. Describe the effect of venous return, plasma electrolytes, stress and exercise on cardiac functions.

12. Discuss the short-term and long-term homeostatic control of blood pressure and the effect of general factors on blood pressure (include baroreceptors, vasomotor centre, cardiac centre, reflex control; renal and hormonal control including adrenaline and renin-angiotensin-aldosterone, etc).
13. Describe how blood pressure can be affected by stress, exercise etc.
14. Define circulatory shock; briefly describe the types and the signs and events of hypovolemic shock.

15. 1. Explain the function of the respiratory system and the processes of respiration pulmonary ventilation, external and internal respiration, transport of blood gases, cellular respiration

2. Describe the functional anatomy of the organs of the respiratory system location, structure and function of the nose and paranasal sinuses, the pharynx, larynx, trachea, the bronchial tree, the lungs and pleural membranes.
3. Differentiate between the organs of the conducting and respiratory zones and between the upper and lower respiratory tract.
4. Describe the pathway of air through the nose to the lungs in relation to the conduction of air, protective mechanisms, and production of sound.
5. Describe the structure of the alveoli (alveoli, respiratory membrane, and surfactant in relation to protection and gaseous exchange.
6. Define the lung volumes and capacities and explain their clinical significance.

7. Describe the process of pulmonary ventilation in relation to pressure and volume changes and the factors that affect pulmonary ventilation such as airway resistance, surface tension, lung compliance, negative intrapleural pressure.
8. Explain the difference in the composition of atmospheric air and alveolar air.

10. Describe the processes of internal respiration and factors that affect gas exchange.

12. Describe the transport of carbon dioxide in the blood according to chemical changes that occur and the factors that affect transport of blood carbon dioxide.

14. Discuss the chemical factors that influence the rate and depth of ventilation e.g. Pco2 , pH, and Po2.
15. Discuss the effect of emotions and conscious control on the rate and depth of breathing e.g. Hypothalamic and cortical control of breathing.
16. Discuss the effect of exercise, body temperature, pain, and irritation to air passageways on the rate and depth of ventilation.

Much of the heart is cardiac muscle (myocardium). Unlike the skeletal muscle cells, cardiac muscle cells generate their own electrical impulses and conduct these impulses (action potentials) to the entire myocardium. These do not occur over the entire heart simultaneously; instead, different parts of the heart are depolarised to different extents at any instant in time. This causes small electric currents to flow in the extracellular fluid from one part of the body to another. These currents can be detected by placing sensitive electrodes on certain parts of the body. A recording of these currents forms an electrocardiogram (ECG).
By convention, the pairs of electrodes are placed in a certain order to give a series of ECG readings. Three of these are shown below.
Any potential difference (voltage) between each pair of electrodes will be amplified and then recorded by an electrocardiograph machine, as a series of up-and-down waves called deflection waves.

Joint surfaces, fitting perfectly into one another, are covered in hyaline cartilage to absorb shock and make movement smooth and painless. Synovial fluid lubricates the hyaline cartilage to facilitate frictionless movement.

Too little synovial fluid, worn away cartilage, injury and diseases (like rheumatoid- and osteoarthritis) can all contribute to inflammation, swelling and joint pain. Damaged cartilage exposes bone ends so that they grind on one another, leading to the formation of bone spurs, as body tries to heal it (causing ill-fitting joint surfaces and more friction).
The periosteum plays an important role in bone growth and bone healing. That is where osteoblasts are found.

A lever consists of a rigid arm, which is free to turn about a fixed point called the fulcrum. The fulcrum is a pivot point.
Components of a lever system – in this case a first-class lever system with the fulcrum in the middle.

Use a pencil as a fulcrum, a ruler as a lever and an eraser as the load. Effort will be provided by your finger to demonstrate how moving the fulcrum closer to or further away from the load effects the force needed to move the load. Do you agree with the following conclusion? Explain.
The closer the fulcrum to the load, the less force needed to lift the load. The closer the fulcrum to the force, the greater the force needed to lift the load.
Levers are divided into three types, or classes, according to the way the load and force arms are arranged around the fulcrum.

In a first-class lever, the FULCRUM (PIVOT) is in the Middle (see image above). When the fulcrum is midway between the force and the load, there is no change in force, speed or distance. If the fulcrum is closer to the load, big mechanical advantage is obtained.
Select and mark the first-class levers from the examples below: The question to ask is: WHAT IS IN THE MIDDLE? First class, look for the ones with the FULCRUM in the middle.
In the second-class lever, the load arm lies between the fulcrum and the force arm. In other words, the LOAD is in the middle.
The fulcrum is usually closer to the load, which reduces the force needed to accomplish the work.
A wheelbarrow can be seen as a second-class lever. List some other examples of the second-class lever:

In this class of levers, the EFFORT lies between the fulcrum and the load. Because of this a relatively large force is required to move the load. This is offset by the fact that it is possible to produce movement of the load over a long distance with a relatively small movement of the force arm. In a third-class lever there is usually a loss in force needed to accomplish the work, but a gain in speed or distance. When a cricket bat or golf club is swung, a third-class lever system acts.

The elbow acts as a fulcrum in both cases and the hands provide the force (hence the lower arm becomes part of the lever). The load (i.e. the puck or the ball) is moved at the end of the stick or bat.

The nervous system is one of the two major control systems of the human body (what is the other?). It consists of the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord) and the peripheral nervous system (spinal and cranial nerves).
Nervous tissue consists of two main types of cells:
neurons - the functional cells of the nervous system, and
neuroglia - the supporting cells. There are multiple types of neurons and neuroglial cells.
The functioning of the nervous system can be divided into three parts:
Sensory function - the detection of changes in the internal and external environment.
Integrative function - the interpretation and decision-making functions.
Motor function - the initiation of actions in response to these changes e.g. muscular contraction or glandular secretions.

The human body has what is called set points – this is where the body maintains homeostasis to, what your body thinks is normal. These set points will be slightly different between people. Sometimes, if your body has something that is constantly outside the normal range (e.g. if your BP is always high), your body changes its set point (it kind of goes, ahh fine, this is what normal is now) to your new normal. This is similar to when people from Dunedin laugh when Aucklanders say it’s cold, and they’re like, THIS ISNT COLD UNTIL YOUR TOILET IS FROZEN, GET IN THE BIN YOU WUSS. These two individuals have different ‘set points’ about what is cold.

Cardiac cycle | Patton: FIGURE 28-19 | The cardiac cycle. | Atrial systole. | Contraction (systole) of the atrial musculature. | Creates a pressure gradient that pushes blood out of the atria into the relaxed ventricles where the pressure is lower. | Isovolumetric ventricular contraction. | During the brief period of isovolumetric ventricular contraction, the intraventricular pressure begins to increase. close the atrioventricular valves—producing the first heart sound—but not enough to overcome arterial pressure and open the semilunar valves. This phase occurs between the start of ventricular systole and the opening of the semilunar valves, during which ventricular volume remains constant as the pressure increases rapidly. | Ejection. | The semilunar valves open and blood is ejected from the heart when the pressure in the ventricles exceeds the pressure in the pulmonary artery and aorta. An initial, shorter phase, called rapid ejection , is characterized by a marked increase in ventricular and aortic pressure and in aortic blood flow. The T wave of the ECG appears during the later, longer phase of reduced ejection (characterized by a less abrupt decrease in ventricular volume). A considerable quantity of blood, called the residual volume, normally remains in the ventricles at the end of the ejection period. In heart failure the residual volume remaining in the ventricles may greatly exceed that ejected during systole. | Isovolumetric ventricular relaxation. | Ventricular diastole, or relaxation, begins with the isovolumetric ventricular relaxation period of the cardiac cycle. It is the period between closure of the semilunar valves and opening of the atrioventricular valves. At the end of ventricular ejection, the semilunar valves close when the ventricular pressure drops below arterial pressure and pushes the valve flaps closed. As the valves snap shut, they produce the second heart sound. Closure of the semilunar valves prevents blood from re-entering the ventricular chambers from the pulmonary trunk and aorta. Both sets of valves are closed, and the ventricles are relaxing. | Ventricular relaxation causes a dramatic fall in intraventricular pressure but not enough to open the atrioventricular valves. Because the valves are closed, there is no change in volume. The atrioventricular valves do not open until the pressure in the atrial chambers increases above that in the relaxing ventricles. | Passive ventricular filling. | As the ventricles continue to relax, the intraventricular pressure continues to drop. That, along with rising | intraatrial | pressure produced by return of venous blood, produces a pressure gradient sufficient to force open the atrioventricular valves. Blood then rushes into the relaxing ventricles. | The rapid influx of blood into the ventricles lasts about 0.1 second and results in a dramatic increase in ventricular volume. The term diastasis is often used to describe a later, longer period of slow ventricular filling as ventricular diastole ends. The abrupt inflow of blood that occurred immediately after opening of the atrioventricular valves is followed by a slow but continuous flow of venous blood into the atria and then through the open atrioventricular valves into the ventricles. It is important to know what your textbook has to offer. Reading a textbook is a lot different than reading a novel. Active reading requires you to think critically – decide for example which information is important or not. The goal of active reading is to enhance your own knowledge and help you do well.

The Marieb text is a great resource for knowledge, to answer questions and to explore relationships between ideas and to apply this knowledge. This is different to being a passive reader who assumes the book will magically “teach” them everything they need to know to pass! An active reader knows that it is their job to get the information from the book and into their head.

Spinal Nerves and the Spinal Cord

The spinal cord and spinal nerves represent one of the transition points from CNS to PNS. The spinal cord is comprised for grey and white matter, and I like to imagine it as looking like a butterfly within an overdrawn set of lips! It's certainly a stretch but can you see it?

The butterfly is the grey matter - this is where the cell bodies of neurons are, and you can see the grey matter is found in the middle, the opposite to the brain! The lips are the white matter tracts, the axons of those neurons connecting the brain to the body! On the image below it shows the different parts of the white matter, the nerve tracts, with the blue part carrying information TO the brain, and the red parts carrying information FROM the brain. You can see it's very distinctly organised! It is not important to remember these tracts, I just wanted you to see how specific each part of the nervous system is!
The spinal nerves are associated with the vertebrae of the spinal column, with the spinal nerves exiting the spinal cord and moving into the body/nerve plexuses through the spaces between vertebrae.
At this junction you have nerves exiting the vertebral column along with blood vessels. This area is an important structure for understanding about reflexes and the reflex arc!

Below you can see how the spinal nerves is arranged, carrying both somatic (voluntary) and visceral (involuntary) motor nerves to control the body. There are two images, showing slightly different views of what the nerve looks like! Both of these examples would be for a nerve of the sympathetic nervous system, and preganglionic fibres as part of the autonomic nervous systems!
The Autonomic nervous system; which covers the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous system includes SOME but not ALL of the peripheral nerves. The image below shows the origins of the SNS and PSNS

The PSNS has a craniosacral origin - from 4 cranial nerves (3, 7, 9 and 10) and 3 sacral spinal nerves (S2-S4). The SNS has what we call a thoracolumbar origin - from T1-L2, the thoracic and lumbar nerves, and forms a chain of sympathetic ganglia (a ganglion/ganglia is just a group of neurons!)
You already know most of the functions of the autonomic nervous system and show be able to rattle off the things that the SNS and PSNS cause in the body.
List as many functions of the SNS and PSNS as you can - including where vasoconstriction and vasodilation will occur!

While there are 31 spinal nerves, there is not an exact one to one relationship with the vertebrae, partly due to the fusion of vertebrae to form the tailbone. The spinal cord has some changes in structure too, forming the cauda equina, named because it looks a bit like a horses tail.

The reflex arc allows the peripheral nervous system to stimulate predictable action in the body. What I mean by this that a reflex is a consistent response to a particular stimulus. Since the response is consistent, the same every time, you can hardwire it into the spinal cord, so you don't need the brain involved in that decision. We do this using interneurons. Gustation (our sense of taste) and Olfaction (our sense of smell) are caleld chemical senses, as they involve receptors on sensory neurons binding to chemical compounds and sending signals to our brains for processing. These are one of the ways that we get information about our world, and chemical senses are thought to be the oldest kind of sense in the world. Even bacteria have the ability to sense the chemicals in the environment around them. For humans, we tend to think of these are less important senses, as we rely heavily on vision and hearing, but, these senses are still important and amazing processes!

The Olfactory Bulb are two structures of the brain that lay on the underside of the brain, and neurons from the olfactory bulbs poke down, through the skull into the roof of the nasal cavity, where volatile compounds (those things that we smell) come into contact with the receptors on the neurons!

An interesting thing about the olfactory bulb is that the neurons are able to be replaced, and are part of something called the rostral migratory stream, where stem cells from the subventricular zone (near the ventricles of the brain) grow and divide to create cells that will travel to the olfactory bulb to replace old cells. And this was actually discovered by a research group here in NZ!

Our body has calcium homeostasis, where it keeps the concentration of calcium in the blood is kept the same, either by storing calcium away in the body, or by releasing calcium from the body stores and input/output systems.

We can name the connections between muscles and bones based on their function. I'm a big fan of looking at different pieces of content in this kind of format, to help keep things interesting! There are many many endocrine organs in the body.

The job of the endocrine system is to help in homeostasis and regulation of the body and works closely alongside the nervous system. In fact, there are similarities and differences between these systems! The nervous system tends to have a rapid response, but a short lived action, whereas the endocrine system tends to take a little longer to get started, but has a longer lasting effect.

You've actually come across this before - the regulation of blood pressure is controlled by the brain to regulate BP immediately, and hormones (the Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone pathway) over the long term.

which means to secrete. Endocrine organs secrete hormones (a special chemical signal in the body) into the bloodstream, where they can travel around the body and have an action and effect on the body. This is different to exocrine glands, which secrete something onto a surface (like sweat glands secreting sweat, or the liver that secretes digestive bile onto the surface of the inside of the duodenum).

8. How is glucose stored in the body, and where?

Just like your kitchen, you have 3 places to put glucose. The pantry is for short term storage (for ready to eats, or snacks!) where the glucose is easily available, the fridge for longer term storage (where you put ingredients, things you gotta do stuff to to make a meal), for use over the day inbetween meals, and the deep freezer, where you store things for a LONG time, and only utilse once you've run out of the easy stuff (like when you freexe leftovers for when you can't be bothered cooking, or you store a ham cos you got in cheap and are saving it for Christmas).

The pantry of your body is your muscle, which stores glucose as glycogen (the storage form of glucose, which creates long branching chains, kind of like starch!). The glycogen in your muscles can be used BY your muscles, and is immediately available once it is broken down. Kind of like having snacks in your pocket!

The fridge of your body is the liver - the liver stores glucose as glycogen as well but does so for the rest of the body, so inbetween meals, your liver can release glucose into your blood for the other parts of your body to use. That nagging hungry feeling you get after a few hours is normally your liver singalling that it's running out of stored glucose!

The deep freeze of your body is your fat. Glucose is converted into fatty acids for long term storage, as your can store more calories as fat than as glycogen in the same amount of space. Your body likes to have fat stores for energy, as our bodies don't know that in the winter the supermarket is still open, and you liekly have blankets and maybe a heater to keep you warm!

17. What is the difference between steroid and non-steroid hormones?

The bulk of our hormones are non-steroidal. They can be made from amino acids, polypeptides or proteins and cannot cross the cell membrane, so need a cell surface receptor, and create a intracellular cascade (it is kind of the equivalent of someone coming to your door and shouting instructions!). Steroid hormones are lipid soluble, so are able to diffuse through the cell membrane and enter cells. This means that they don't need a cell surface receptor and instead can travel to the nucleus where they change gene activation. This means that they can turn genes on or off, so during puberty, our hormones actually turn genes on, which is why our bodies can change so dramatically!

Complete the genetics glossary below. They are in no particular order, and some related words are close together in the list, or further apart!

The process of cell division that results in 2 genetically identical (but not necessarily functionally identical) daughter cells. These daughter cells will have 46 chromosomes (23 pairs), and they will be diploid (having 2 set of chromosomes, 1 maternal and 1 paternal).

The process of cell division that results in 4 genetically varied daughter cells that function as gametes (egg cells and sperm cells). Only occurs in your gonads, and each daughter cell will have 23 chromosomes (1 set) and haploid (1 set chromosomes).

The fact that humans have different versions of genes, and their complement of genes (that make up their genome) can be very different to others. This variation is important for health and wellbeing. When populations have low genetic variation, they can be more susceptible to disease and genetic issues.
A sequence of DNA that codes for a protein. That protein will carry out a function in the body!
The genetic material that contains all the instructions for the body's function.
DNA isn't found by itself, in the nucleus, it is package up and wound around special proteins. These proteins and DNA together are called chromatin.
A chromosome is a length of DNA that is inherited together - certain genes are found on certain chromosomes! Humans have 46 chromosomes, 23 from mum and 23 from dad.
A chromosome that is not a sex chromosome and so does not contribute to genetic sex. Autosomes in humans are numbered 1-22

A chromosome that contributes to genetic sex. In humans these are the X and Y chromosome, and most people have 2, a pair of sex chromosomes, with an X from mum, and either an X or Y from dad (but there are other genetic sex combos as well!).
A cell with only one of each chromosome. Our gametes (eggs and sperm) are haploid and have 23 chromosomes
A cell with 2 of each chromosome. Our body cells are diploid and have 23 pairs of chromosomes, for a total of 46 chromosomes.

When a person has an abnormal number of chromsomes - usually an extra, or missing 1. There are a few different aneuploidies, but common ones are Down Syndrome (or Trisomy 21 when a person inherits an extra chromosome 21), Turners syndrome (when a person have only 1 sex chromosome and so their genetic sex is XO), or Klinefelters syndrome (when a person has 2 X chromosomes and 1 Y chromsome).

Polyploid is when something has multiple SETS of chromosomes, and can be triploid (3 copies of each chromosome), tetraploid (4) and so on. This is very rare in human reproduction, but can occur in liver and placenta cells!

Disjunction is when chromosomes divide during meiosis. In meiosis 2, sister chromatids that make up a chromosome are split into 2 new chromosomes, and end up in different gametes. When this doesn't happen properly, it is called non-disjunction, and gametes end up with extra chromosomes or missing chromosomes (ie 1 gametes gets 2 chromosomes, and the other gamete made in the same division gets none!)
The process by which a cell splits into two new cells. The parent cells must be large enough and have duplicates of their DNA and organelles so the two new cells have their own machinery.
The different stages of mitosis (and meiosis)
In humans, this is a haploid sex cell that will be used for sexual reproduction - a male and female gamete join to create a zygote!

A version of a gene that is always present in a phenotype (the traits/things that we see in our body). The dominant allele is like your loud friend, if they are there, you're always going to hear them!

A version of a gene that you only see in the phemotype or trait of a person if there is none of the dominant version. The reccessive allele is like that friend you have that everyone think is shy and quiet, but as soon as everyone leaves, they turn into the nutjob you know and love :)

When you have codominance, you have 2 dominant alleles. So that is like having two loud friends, and they just talk over each other all the time! There are traits we have where 2 version can be expressed at the same time. The best example is human blood groups. A and B alleles are both dominant, which is why you have A blood, B blood AND AB blood which has both. O blood group is the recessive!

Incomplete dominance is when you have two alleles, and neither one is really properly dominant. A good example is flowers, where you have a red version, and a white version of the gene for colour, but when you have BOTH versions you end up with pink! SO not quite red, not quite white. You dont see this much in humans, Sickle Cell disease is really the only example. In Sickle cell disease, if you have both a normal gene and a disease gene, half your RBCS are sickle shaped and half are normal. This mix means a person won't have the symptoms of sickle cell disease (which is bad), but! they are resistant to malaria!
When 1 gene creates a trait. Some examples of monogenic traits are: Attached or unattached ear lobes, middle digit hair, where there distinct options, or groups of traits.

When multiple genes create a trait. Some examples of polygenetic traits are things that have a spectrum, like height, body size, hair colour, body shape, eye colour, voice, skin colour - there isn't necessarily specific groups, e.g. blonde vs brown is subjective.

Are what we call the different versions of genes, and they can be recessive or dominant! For example, a gene could have a normal and diseased version - they would each be alleles. We commonly use eye colour alleles to think about this too.

Blood pressure is determined by several factors related to both the heart and blood vessels. It is the force that blood exerts on the walls of arteries as it is pumped by the heart. Blood pressure is influenced by:
: The amount of blood the heart pumps per minute. The higher the cardiac output, the higher the blood pressure.
: The resistance that blood encounters as it flows through blood vessels, mainly in the arteries. If arteries constrict (narrow), resistance increases, and so does blood pressure.
: The total amount of blood in the circulatory system. More blood increases pressure.
: Thicker blood (higher viscosity) increases resistance and, consequently, blood pressure.
: Healthy, flexible arteries allow for more efficient blood flow. If the arteries become stiff (e.g., due to arteriosclerosis), blood pressure can rise.

2. What is the structure of a lymph nodes, and what is found in lymph nodes?
The lymph node is enclosed by a fibrous outer layer called the capsule. This provides structural support and protection for the node.

The outer region of the lymph node is called the cortex. The cortex contains clusters of immune cells called B lymphocytes and follicles (also called lymphoid follicles), where B-cells are activated in response to antigens.

Beneath the cortex is the paracortex, which contains T lymphocytes (T-cells). This area is also where the immune cells are activated by antigens and where interactions between B-cells and T-cells occur.

The medulla is the inner portion of the lymph node. It contains medullary cords, which are made up of lymphocytes (mainly B-cells), macrophages, and plasma cells. This is where the final steps of immune responses take place, including the production of antibodies.

The lymph node contains sinuses, which are channels that allow lymph to flow through the node. These sinuses help filter out pathogens, debris, and other foreign particles as the lymph flows through the node.

Lymph enters the node through afferent lymphatic vessels and exits through efferent lymphatic vessels. The afferent vessels bring lymph from the tissues, while the efferent vessels drain filtered lymph away from the node.
What is Found in Lymph Nodes?
B lymphocytes (B-cells): These are found primarily in the cortex and are responsible for producing antibodies in response to pathogens.
T lymphocytes (T-cells): Found mainly in the paracortex, T-cells help in recognizing and killing infected cells or coordinating the immune response.
Macrophages: Found throughout the lymph node, these cells help engulf and digest pathogens and debris.
Plasma cells: These are activated B-cells that have differentiated to secrete antibodies.

The fluid that circulates through the lymphatic system, carrying white blood cells, proteins, waste products, and sometimes pathogens or foreign particles, which the immune cells within the lymph node work to filter and destroy.

Aims BN2 BNP2 BNM2 This course will lay the foundations of scientific knowledge required for future nursing practice including the basic structure, concepts and principles that underpin functioning of the human body. The purpose of this course is to continue the development of the scientific knowledge required for future nursing practice. The purpose of this course is to examine and apply Maatai Oranga (Health Science) in relation to Tikanga aa-Tapuhi. Learning Outcomes BN2 BNP2 BNM2 On successful completion of this course, students will be able to: • LO1 : Explain the structure and function of a range of human body systems to support safe nursing practice. • LO2 : Analyse the principles of homeostasis in maintaining physiological balance relevant to nursing care. • LO3 : Describe the support, coordination and control of movement in the human body within a nursing context. • LO4 : Apply knowledge of human genetics and inheritance to nursing assessment and care planning. • LO5 : Demonstrate knowledge of the regulatory and integrative functions of the human body including sensory functions, to underpin nursing practice. 29 MIT| Nursing & Health Studies| 722.537 | 722.541 | 722.552 | 2026 (2) Section C: Electrocardiogram Much of the heart is cardiac muscle (myocardium). Unlike the skeletal muscle cells, cardiac muscle cells generate their own electrical impulses and conduct these impulses (action potentials) to the entire myocardium. These do not occur over the entire heart simultaneously; instead, different parts of the heart are depolarised to different extents at any instant in time. This causes small electric currents to flow in the extracellular fluid from one part of the body to another. These currents can be detected by placing sensitive electrodes on certain parts of the body. A recording of these currents forms an electrocardiogram (ECG). By convention, the pairs of electrodes are placed in a certain order to give a series of ECG readings. Three of these are shown below. Lead I ................................................... Left Arm-Right Arm Lead II .................................................. Right Arm-Left Leg Lead III ................................................. Left Arm-Left Leg Any potential difference (voltage) between each pair of electrodes will be amplified and then recorded by an electrocardiograph machine, as a series of up-and-down waves called deflection waves. Clinical applications • Joint surfaces, fitting perfectly into one another, are covered in hyaline cartilage to absorb shock and make movement smooth and painless. Synovial fluid lubricates the hyaline cartilage to facilitate frictionless movement. • Too little synovial fluid, worn away cartilage, injury and diseases (like rheumatoid- and osteoarthritis) can all contribute to inflammation, swelling and joint pain. Damaged cartilage exposes bone ends so that they grind on one another, leading to the formation of bone spurs, as body tries to heal it (causing ill-fitting joint surfaces and more friction). • The periosteum plays an important role in bone growth and bone healing. 2 1. Blood pressure Jack and Jill have blood pressure issues. Jack has high blood pressure, and has been talking quinapril for about 1 year, and their GP has just added metoprolol to their prescription. Jack has been told they may need to be mindful of standing too quickly, as Jack might get a bit dizzy or even pass out; something called postural hypotension. Jack is really mindful, as their Dad had to get an angiogram, and then a bypass in a coronary vessel due to blocked coronary vessels and angina. Jill, on the other hand, has been having dizzy spells, and excessive thirst. They were admitted to hospital, and vitals were taken showing a bp of 80/55, with concentrated, low volume urine being noted by the admitting nurse. As a student nurse, you’ll need a robust understanding of how the cardiovascular system works, to understand what is happening for each of these people. 1. What determines blood pressure? You’ll need to think about our physiology as well as those factors that can change our blood pressure. 2. High blood pressure is defined as? 3. High blood pressure has several chronic, downstream consequences. What are they? Thinking about the implications for long term health and wellness, as well as why we care as nurses! 4. Low blood pressure has several acute consequences. These are? You have nervous system processes that help to keep your blood pressure steady at rest, and help to increase or decrease it back to normal for exercise or after exercise, based on feedback from your body. We are going to focus on regulation – how your body RETURNS blood pressure to normal after it has been changed. 5. How does the nervous system detect and return blood pressure to normal when it is lower than normal (e.g. you’ve just stood up quickly and BP to your brain drops; think gravity – as for Jack’s postural hypotension) 6. How is this process different when it is higher than normal (e.g. after a run, after a fright, etc) You also have renal system processes that use hormones to help return low blood pressure to normal over the long term. 7. The kidneys normally help to increase blood pressure if it is too low – this is a slower process (which takes minutes to hours, depending on the circumstances). Explain how this occurs. The human body has what is called set points – this is where the body maintains homeostasis to, what your body thinks is normal. These set points will be slightly different between people. Sometimes, if your body has something that is constantly outside the normal range (e.g. if your BP is always high), your body changes its set point (it kind of goes, ahh fine, this is what normal is now) to your new normal. This is similar to when people from Dunedin laugh when Aucklanders say it’s cold, and they’re like, THIS ISNT COLD UNTIL YOUR TOILET IS FROZEN, GET IN THE BIN YOU WUSS. These two individuals have different ‘set points’ about what is cold. 8. What are Jack’s medications trying to do? Explain in plain, easy to understand language! Relate it back to the processes you described in question 6 and 7! 9. Why are medications for high blood pressure started when there are no symptoms of damage? Atherosclerosis is the process by which blood vessels can become narrowed, because a fatty plaque builds up in the blood vessel. This narrowing can prevent blood flowing though the vessel, and even end up blocking the vessel. If this happens in the coronary vessels, this can cause angina, chest pain, or worse! 10. Where does the fatty deposit build up? 11. What does narrowing a blood vessel and preventing/restriction blood flow cause? What are some examples of these around the body?

16/03/2021 16 Q15: Outline the processes involved in renal regulation of blood pressure to correct low blood pressure You should include: - Indirect mechanisms - Direct mechanisms Q15: Renal BP • 1. The kidney has its own barorecepetor, called the juxtaglomerular apparatus which are cells in the kidney. • 2. When the juxtaglomerular apparatus senses a change in blood pressure, it will initiate regulatory mechanisms. The kidney acts primarily to increase the blood pressure - if the blood pressure is high, the following steps will NOT take place. Direct mechanism: 3A. There is a reduction in the glomerular filtration rate (or GFR), so the kidney slows the rate which it is filtering the blood. 4A. When the filtration slows down, urine production also slows down. This results in fluid being maintained in the blood. 5A. This increases the blood volume 6A. Blood volume is directly tied to blood pressure, as a higher volume of fluid will stretch the blood vessels, causing blood pressure to increase. Indirect mechanism: happens at the same time as the direct mechanism 3B. As the kidney is slowing its filtration rate, the kidney also releases Renin. Renin is an enzyme and converts Angiotensinogen from the liver to Angiotensin I 4B. Angiotensin I travels to the lungs where ACE (Angiotensin converting enzyme) converts Angiotensin I to Angiotension II 5B. Angiotensin II (Ang II) impacts multiple parts of the body to restore normal blood pressure. i) Ang II leads to vasoconstriction. As the vessels constrict, the resistance inside them increases, which causes peripheral resistance (PR, or systemic vascular resistance SVR) to increase. ii) Ang II increases the release of ADH (anti-diuretic hormone). ADH acts of the collecting ducts of the nephron making it more porous. This causes more water to be reabsorbed from the filtrate (which will become urine) back into the blood. This causes the blood volume to increase. iii) Ang II acts on the adrenal gland to cause the release of Aldosterone. Aldosterone is a hormone that acts on the nephron to increase the resabsorption of Na+ from the filtrate into the blood. As water always follows salt, this causes more water to be absorbed into the blood. This causes the blood volume to increase. 6B. The increase in peripheral resistance (from vasoconstriction) and the increase in blood volume help to increase the blood pressure back to normal.
